Analysis · Quantz · Flute Concerto in G Major, QV 5:174 · Movement I

I. Allegro Assai

A ritornello movement built almost exactly the way Quantz tells composers to build one in his Versuch (1752): a two-part opening tutti, four solos that move from G to D, E minor and back, short tutti cuts that quote the ritornello, a cadenza on the six-four, and an ending made of the ritornello’s second part. Below: the form, every cadence, the partimento patterns behind the solos and a performance layer for the flute, all on a playable full score.

  • 156 bars, common time
  • 5 ritornellos, 4 solos
  • Keys G → D → E minor → G
  • 33 cadences marked
  • 61 pattern brackets

Form at a Glance

Ritornellos (blue) and solos (amber), the key areas, and below them where each instrument plays: the solo flute, the strings of the tutti, and the basso continuo. Click a section to find it on the score.

Ritornello (tutti)SoloFlute (solo)StringsBasso continuo

The ritornello has two parts, as Quantz requires (XVIII §33, rule 8): Part 1 (mm. 1–13) returns at the start of Ritornellos 2 and 4, Part 2 (mm. 14–23) at the start of Ritornello 3 and, complete, as Ritornello 5. The basso drops out under many solo passages, and Violin II or the viola takes the bass (bassetto). Section boundaries and keys are our reading ours.

Cadences

Every cadence marked on the score, with the evidence from the bass and the figures. All labels are our reading ours.

  • Half cadences close the first phrase of each tonic ritornello (m. 7, echoed m. 9; m. 60 in D), open each Ponte (mm. 36, 82, 142) and give the soloist a fermata for a lead-in in m. 117.
  • Six-four cadences (cadenza composta): the main cadences are approached by a bass rising step by step to 5 and a 64 → 53 on it (mm. 20–21, 22–23, 50–54, 62–65, 93, 127–130, 133–135, 146–147, 153–156).
  • Evaded cadences: Ritornello 1 and Ritornello 5 both swerve from V to vi (bass E) before the final close (mm. 23, 156), and Solo 2 swerves to C before its cadence in E minor (m. 86).
  • Echo cadences: Quantz pairs forte and piano statements (mm. 8–9, 19, 21, 52, 92); the piano one never ends a section.
  • Elision: the flute enters on the cadence that ends a ritornello (mm. 65, 93.3, 115).
  • Keys reached by cadence: D major (mm. 12, 47, 54, 65), E minor (mm. 77, 87, 93), G major (mm. 23, 99, 109, 125, 130, 147, 156).

Partimento Patterns

The bass patterns under every bar, named with partimento and galant terms (the rule of the octave, Gjerdingen’s schemata). Each reading rests on the bass line and Quantz’s figures; where the basso rests, on the string part that carries the bass. The names are modern labels, not Quantz’s guideline. The buttons scroll to the place and play it.

Opening

Tonic Pedal

Four bars of G in the bass with IV (64), then ii (42) and V (F♯ with 65) above: the ritornello states the key before it moves. In the solos the pedal moves up into Violin II (mm. 24–27, 118–121).

Cadence

Cadenza Composta

1–2–3–4–5 by step, then 64 → 53 on 5. It closes Ritornello 1 (mm. 20, 22), the first solo (mm. 50–53, in D), Ritornello 3 (m. 93, in E minor) and the last solo (mm. 127–129, in G). The plain cadenza semplice, without the six-four, ends Solo 2 (m. 86).

Sequence

Rising 5–6

Bass C–D–E–F♯ with 5 then 6 on each note (mm. 17–18): the climb in Part 2 of the ritornello.

Schema

Romanesca

D–A, B–F♯, G–D (1–5, 6–3, 4–1) in Violin II (mm. 39–41), and G–D, E–B, C–G in the viola (mm. 135–137): both times in the bassetto, under flute arpeggios. Its stepwise form, a falling octave in tenths, follows in mm. 47–48 and 125–126.

Schema

Passo Indietro

4 with 4♯2 stepping back to 3 with 6: twice in Solo 1 (in A, then D, mm. 41–44) and twice in Solo 4 (in D, then G, mm. 137–140), each time followed by a suspension over the bass.

Schema

Ponte

A held dominant before an arrival: A for D (mm. 36–38), B for E minor (mm. 82–84), D for G (mm. 132–134, in tied whole notes).

Schema

Monte

B–C, C♯–D, D♯–E in Violin II (mm. 74–77): each step up reached through its own leading tone, the way from G into E minor.

Sequence

Circle of Fifths

E–A–D–G–C–F♯–B (mm. 79–82), faster in Violin II in mm. 95–96, and B–E–A–D–G back to G (mm. 102–103).

Schema

Fonte (Lengthened)

A, G, F♯, E, each reached from its leading tone with 65 (mm. 89–91): a Fonte stretched to four steps, inside Ritornello 3.

Performing the Flute Part

The blue marks above the flute staff apply Quantz’s rules on breathing, tonguing and dynamics to this movement ours; the red marks above them are the printed marks of the Suzuki Flute School edition revised by Toshio Takahashi, for comparison. Hover any mark for its source. Both layers can be switched off above the score.

Rules We Apply Quantz

Paraphrased from the Versuch, chapters VI (tonguing), VII (breathing), XI and XII (the Allegro) and XV (cadenzas), Reilly pp. 71–185.

  • Breath ’: take it from a long note, never from a short one or the last note of a bar (p. 87); before a new idea (p. 88); in running sixteenths after the first note of a group, which is shortened; a wide leap is the best place (p. 89). Rests give the breath for free.
  • Eighths short, quarters sung: in an Allegro assai whose quickest notes are sixteenths, the eighths are tongued briefly and the quarters played singing and sustained (XII §22, p. 133). Leaps and repeated notes take ti, the short firm stroke (p. 73).
  • ti‿ti ri ti: when sixteenths are too quick for diri, slur the first two notes and tongue the third with ri and the fourth with ti; Quantz recommends this above the other ways (p. 78).
  • did’ll: the double tongue, for the quickest passage-work only (pp. 79–80). At ♩ = 160 the sixteenths here are eight to a pulse beat, the limit Quantz sets (p. 284).
  • Echo: a repeated figure changes dynamic, Piano after Forte (p. 133). Swell: long notes grow and fade (p. 132). Accent: dissonant appoggiaturas and suspensions louder than their resolution (pp. 254–255), and the low note of a deep leap stronger (p. 132).
  • Cadenza: on a wind instrument it must fit in one breath (XV §17, p. 185).

Takahashi’s Edition comparison

Printed marks only (pages 6–8 of the flute part); the handwritten notes in the copy are left out. Breitkopf, the source of our score, prints almost nothing in the solos beyond slurs on a few figures and the p and f of the echo bars.

They agree on the breaths (17 of Takahashi’s 18 at the same place; at m. 74 he splits the tie), on the echo in m. 83, and on the sung, separated quarters at the ends of phrases. They differ most on the slurs in the sixteenth passages, on which note of a leap to stress, on register (three passages an octave up) and on the cadenza, which Takahashi writes out with a breath inside it.

The Articulation View

Choose Articulation above the score for three flute staves over the bass: Fl., the part as Breitkopf prints it; Fl. Q., our Quantz reading engraved as notation ours; and Fl. T., Takahashi’s printed marks. Only Fl. Q. sounds at first; turn on Fl. or Fl. T. to hear the others.

  • Fl. Q.: in the passages we read as ti with sung quarters, a staccato dot on each unslurred eighth and a tenuto line on each quarter (XII §22, p. 133); a slur over the first two of each four sixteenths where we read ti‿ti ri ti (VI, p. 78); did’ll passages left without slurs, since the tongue does the work; a comma for each breath; an accent on the appoggiaturas and on the low note of a deep leap (pp. 132, 254–255). Breitkopf’s own slurs and strokes stay.
  • Fl. T.: Takahashi’s slurs, portato and tenuto marks, accents and breath marks, his appoggiaturas written out (mm. 26, 115, 120), and the 8va passages written at the pitch he gives. His written trill endings, Eingang and cadenza are left out.
  • The clearest contrasts: the sixteenths of mm. 35–41 and 75–84, which Quantz slurs two and tongues two, while Takahashi slurs whole groups or tongues one and slurs three; and the phrase-ending quarters, which Quantz sings (tenuto) and Takahashi marks portato.

Quantz’s Rules and This Movement

Rules Quantz

Paraphrased from Versuch XVIII §33, the first movement of a serious concerto for one solo instrument (Reilly pp. 311–312), and XV on cadenzas.

  • The ritornello needs at least two main sections, and the second ends the movement (rule 8). Here: Part 1 mm. 1–13, Part 2 mm. 14–23, and Ritornello 5 is Part 2 again.
  • A new idea may open the solo if the ritornello’s head is not singing enough (rule 9). Here the flute does not take over the busy arpeggio head; it sings a slower version of it in long notes (m. 24).
  • The best ideas of the ritornello are broken up and mixed into the solos (rule 4). Here: the one-bar tutti cuts of mm. 31, 33, 70, 72 and 77 quote the start of Part 2.
  • Singing and brilliant solo passages alternate, with short, lively tutti between them (rule 10).
  • Accompaniment in the solos is light, sometimes with few parts (rule 12). Here the basso often rests and Violin II or the viola takes the bass line.
  • No key too far away (rule 13). Here: V, vi and back.
  • The last tutti is the second part of the first ritornello, as short as possible (rule 17).
  • A cadenza comes on the penultimate bass note, the fifth of the key (XV §1, Reilly p. 179), is allowed in serious quick pieces (XV §4, p. 180), and on a wind instrument fits in one breath (XV §17, p. 185).
  • Tempo: Allegro assai in common time takes one pulse beat (about 80 a minute) for each half note (XVII.vii §51, Reilly p. 285). The page starts at quarter = 160 for that reason; use the slider to slow it down.

Guidelines and Our Readings guideline ours

  • Pattern names (Romanesca, Ponte, Monte, Fonte, Passo indietro) are Robert Gjerdingen’s, from Music in the Galant Style (2007), applied by us. The rule of the octave, the five-six sequence and the cadenza semplice and composta are partimento teaching terms.
  • Bass in the upper strings. Both Romanescas (mm. 39–41 in Violin II, 135–137 in the viola), the Monte (mm. 74–77) and two circles of fifths (mm. 95–96, 102–103) lie in the bassetto while the basso rests, so the brackets for them sit under those staves.
  • Cadence types (PAC, IAC, HC, evaded) are modern labels. We call a cadence perfect only when the bass goes 5–1 in root position and the melody ends on 1.
  • The m. 117 fermata. Quantz describes fermatas in vocal music and “very rarely” in a solo instrumental part (XV §35, Reilly pp. 193–194): the embellishment uses only notes of the bass chord and does not modulate. That fits a lead-in on the half cadence. The word [Eingang] is the editor’s.
  • Form labels. Calling mm. 1–23 two parts follows Quantz’s rule 8 and the return of mm. 14–23 at the end; where Part 1 ends (m. 13 or m. 9) is our judgment.

Notes on the Reading

The Score

The score follows the Breitkopf edition: five staves (flute, Violin I, Violin II, viola in the alto clef, basso with its figures), with the beams, slurs, strokes, trills, appoggiaturas, dynamics, fermatas and rehearsal letters as printed. Where the violins share a staff in the edition, they are written as two layers.

Flute + Basso Continuo keeps only the outer staves. In the solos this is how the movement sounds with a keyboard realizing the figures; where the basso rests (the bassetto passages, for example mm. 24–30, 39–41, 47–48, 74–77 and 135–137), the bass line of the full score lies in the strings and is missing from this view.

Source and Check

Transcribed from the Breitkopf & Härtel score edited by Horst Augsbach (scan supplied by the user), 156 bars. Each part was read from the scan and checked bar by bar against full-size crops of every system.

Playback: a baroque ensemble at A = 415 by default (flute, violins, viola, cello with harpsichord, each from its own recorded samples), a harpsichord alone at A = 415, or the Steinway Grand at A = 440. Slurred notes are joined, strokes shortened. Trills start on the upper note; appoggiaturas take half the main note (two thirds of a dotted note), following Quantz VIII (Reilly p. 95). The fermata of m. 117 and the cadenza of m. 146 are held, not improvised.
